mechanism: muscle action lowers the pressure inside the sealed cavity; the protuberance helps keep the seal and the pressure difference, giving strong, releasable attachment under water

evidence.citation: Tramacere F, Beccai L, Kuba M, Gozzi A, Bifone A, Mazzolai B (2013). The morphology and adhesion mechanism of Octopus vulgaris suckers. PLoS ONE 8: e65074.
Baik S, Kim DW, Park Y, Lee TJ, Bhang SH, Pang C (2017). A wet-tolerant adhesive patch inspired by protuberances in suction cups of octopi. Nature 546: 396-400.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The animal adds active muscle control and chemical sensing that passive copies lack. Tagged packaging and agrifood for gripping wet or delicate goods on handling lines.

title: Clingfish suction disc: holding on to rough, slimy rock
summary: The northern clingfish lives in surf zones and clings to rocks with a suction disc on its belly. The disc's soft edge is covered in tiny, branched papillae that fill the gaps in rough or fouled surfaces and seal them, and the fish can hold many times its own weight. Suction cups modelled on this disc stick to rough surfaces where ordinary cups leak.
structure: disc with a soft margin covered in hierarchical micro-papillae
mechanism: the compliant, papillae-covered rim conforms to surface roughness and seals, so suction holds even on irregular, slippery surfaces

evidence.citation: Wainwright DK, Kleinteich T, Kleinteich A, Gorb SN, Summers AP (2013). Stick tight: suction adhesion on irregular surfaces in the northern clingfish. Biology Letters 9: 20130234.

Ditsche P, Summers AP (2019). Learning from Northern clingfish (Gobiesox maeandricus): bioinspired suction cups attach to rough surfaces. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 374: 20190204.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Bioinspired cups are prototypes. Tagged water-utilities for fixing sensors or tools to wet, rough or fouled surfaces such as tanks and pipes; this use is our inference, not tested in the sources.

title: Remora disc: hitchhiking on sharks with a friction-boosted suction pad
summary: Remoras ride on sharks, whales and turtles using a suction disc on top of the head, a modified fin. Rows of plate-like lamellae carry tiny spines that catch on the host's skin and raise friction, while a soft lip seals the disc. A robotic disc copying these parts attached to smooth and rough surfaces, including shark skin, under water and was released on demand.
structure: oval disc with rows of movable lamellae bearing small spinules, ringed by a soft fleshy lip
mechanism: the lip seals the disc to hold suction, and the spinules on the raised lamellae engage the surface to add friction against sliding

evidence.citation: Beckert M, Flammang BE, Nadler JH (2015). Remora attachment is enhanced by spinule friction. Journal of Experimental Biology 218: jeb123893.

Wang Y, Yang X, Chen Y, Wainwright DK, Kenaley CP, Gong Z, Liu Z, Liu H, Guan J, Wang T, Weaver JC, Wood RJ, Wen L (2017). A biorobotic adhesive disc for underwater hitchhiking inspired by the remora suckerfish. Science Robotics 2: eaan8072.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Applications so far are research robots and animal-tagging devices; no sector tag is given because no industrial use is documented in the sources.

title: Sandcastle worm cement: glue that sets under seawater
summary: The sandcastle worm builds its tube from sand grains and shell bits glued together under the sea. It secretes a fluid made of oppositely charged proteins that sets into a solid, porous foam bonding the grains. The chemistry has inspired synthetic water-borne adhesives made of paired charged polymers. Because it rests on protein biochemistry, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.
mechanism: oppositely charged adhesive proteins condense into a dense fluid that spreads on wet surfaces and then hardens into a porous solid

evidence.citation: Stewart RJ, Weaver JC, Morse DE, Waite JH (2004). The tube cement of Phragmatopoma californica: a solid foam. Journal of Experimental Biology 207: 4727-4734.
Shao H, Bachus KN, Stewart RJ (2009). A water-borne adhesive modeled after the sandcastle glue of P. californica. Macromolecular Bioscience 9: 464-471.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: relies on protein biochemistry, legal review pending. Synthetic analogues are mainly studied as medical adhesives.

title: Bone: living with cracks by finding and replacing damaged tissue
summary: Everyday loading constantly creates microscopic cracks in bone. Bone tolerates them because its layered structure stops cracks from growing quickly, and because cells detect damaged regions and replace them through remodelling, removing old bone and laying down new. This combination of damage tolerance, detection and targeted repair is a model for self-healing materials and for maintenance strategies that repair before failure.
structure: hierarchical mineralised collagen with interfaces that deflect cracks, and a network of cells throughout
mechanism: microcracks are slowed by the bone's structure while cell networks sense damage and trigger local removal and replacement of the damaged tissue

evidence.citation: Taylor D, Hazenberg JG, Lee TC (2007). Living with cracks: damage and repair in human bone. Nature Materials 6: 263-268.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Repair depends on living cells and blood supply; engineered materials can copy the strategy, not the biology. See lib-0021 for trabecular bone as a lightweight structure.

title: Dutchman's pipe vine: stems that seal their own cracks
summary: As the stem of the Dutchman's pipe vine thickens, its stiff outer ring of tissue tears. Cells from the soft tissue beneath swell into the gap and plug it, and the seal later hardens. Copying this fast first sealing, researchers lined inflatable membranes with a soft foam that closes punctures, keeping the structure under pressure.

common_names: Aristolochia macrophylla (name used in the cited papers)

structure: ring of stiff sclerenchyma around soft, pressurised parenchyma tissue
mechanism: turgid parenchyma cells expand into fissures in the stiff ring and seal them quickly; lignification later restores some strength

evidence.citation: Busch S, Seidel R, Speck O, Speck T (2010). Morphological aspects of self-repair of lesions caused by internal growth stresses in stems of Aristolochia macrophylla and Aristolochia ringens. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 277: 2113-2120.

Rampf M, Speck O, Speck T, Luchsinger RH (2011). Self-repairing membranes for inflatable structures inspired by a rapid wound sealing process of climbing plants. Journal of Bionic Engineering 8: 242-250.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The foam coating seals small punctures only and adds weight; long-term ageing is not reported. Tagged textiles for coated technical fabrics and construction for pneumatic building membranes.

title: Skin-like vascular networks that deliver healing agent to cracks
summary: Skin heals repeatedly because a network of blood vessels brings repair materials to any wound. Engineers copied this with polymer coatings laid over a three-dimensional network of tiny channels filled with liquid healing agent: when a crack reaches the channels, agent flows in and hardens, and the same spot can heal several times. Earlier systems used broken capsules of healing agent, which work only once.
trait: skin and its blood supply (as model)
structure: three-dimensional microchannel network under a polymer coating, filled with a liquid healing agent
mechanism: cracks that reach the network draw healing agent into the damage by capillary action, where it reacts and seals the crack; the network can be refilled

evidence.citation: White SR, Sottos NR, Geubelle PH, Moore JS, Kessler MR, Sriram SR, Brown EN, Viswanathan S (2001). Autonomic healing of polymer composites. Nature 409: 794-797.
Toohey KS, Sottos NR, Lewis JA, Moore JS, White SR (2007). Self-healing materials with microvascular networks. Nature Materials 6: 581-585.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Lab demonstrations; channels reduce stiffness and add manufacturing cost, and healing restores only part of the original strength.

title: Prairie dog burrows: wind-driven ventilation from mounds of different heights
summary: Prairie dogs build mounds around their burrow entrances, and the mounds at the two ends of a burrow often differ in shape and height. Wind blowing over them creates a small pressure difference between the openings, so air is drawn through the tunnel even in a light breeze. It is a classic example of passive, wind-induced ventilation of an underground space.
structure: burrow with two or more openings surrounded by mounds of different height and shape
mechanism: wind speed and pressure differ over the differently shaped openings, so air is pulled in at one end and out at the other

evidence.citation: Vogel S, Ellington CP, Kilgore DL (1973). Wind-induced ventilation of the burrow of the prairie-dog, Cynomys ludovicianus. Journal of Comparative Physiology 85: 1-14.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The same principle is used in wind cowls and stack design; actual flow depends on wind speed and direction, so buildings still need a fallback.

title: Fish gill rakers: filters that do not clog
summary: Many filter-feeding fish do not catch food by trapping it on a sieve. Water flows along their gill rakers rather than straight through, so particles are carried towards the throat and concentrated, while the mesh stays clear. Manta rays go further: particles bounce off their filter lobes back into the flow. These cross-flow and 'ricochet' patterns inspire low-clogging filters for water and food processing.
structure: rows of comb-like rakers or lobes along the mouth cavity, angled to the main water flow
mechanism: flow runs parallel to the filter surface, so particles are swept along and concentrated instead of building up a clogging cake; in mantas, particles rebound off the lobes and stay in the main stream

evidence.citation: Sanderson SL, Cheer AY, Goodrich JS, Graziano JD, Callan WT (2001). Crossflow filtration in suspension-feeding fishes. Nature 412: 439-441.
Divi RV, Strother JA, Paig-Tran EWM (2018). Manta rays feed using ricochet separation, a novel nonclogging filtration mechanism. Science Advances 4: eaat9533.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Industrial cross-flow membrane filtration already exists; the fish add geometry ideas. Ricochet separation was shown in physical models, not yet in industrial filters.

title: Spider slit sensors: detecting tiny strains through cracks
summary: Spiders sense vibrations and leg strain with slit-shaped organs in their exoskeleton near the joints. The slits are tiny, fluid-filled gaps whose width changes when the shell is strained, which nerve cells detect. Engineers copied this with thin metal films on a flexible base that carry controlled nanoscale cracks; as the cracks open and close, electrical resistance changes sharply, giving very sensitive strain and vibration sensors.
structure: arrays of narrow slits in the cuticle near leg joints, each linked to sensory cells
mechanism: small deformations of the exoskeleton change the width of the slits, which concentrates strain and makes it detectable

evidence.citation: Barth FG (2004). Spider mechanoreceptors. Current Opinion in Neurobiology 14: 415-422.
Kang D, Pikhitsa PV, Choi YW, Lee C, Shin SS, Piao L, Park B, Suh KY, Kim TI, Choi M (2014). Ultrasensitive mechanical crack-based sensor inspired by the spider sensory system. Nature 516: 222-226.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Crack-based sensors can drift and wear with repeated cycling; tags reflect possible uses in vehicle and structural monitoring, not tested deployments.

title: Pollia berries and cellulose crystals: brilliant colour from plant fibre
summary: The berries of the African plant Pollia condensata are an intense, glittering blue without any blue pigment. In each cell wall, layers of cellulose fibrils are stacked in a slowly twisting spiral that reflects light of one colour, and the colour stays even in dried fruit. Cellulose nanocrystals from wood or cotton self-assemble into the same twisted structure when a suspension dries, giving plant-based colourants and glitter that could replace dyes and plastic glitter.
structure: cellulose microfibrils stacked in helicoidal (twisted, layered) arrangements
mechanism: the regular helical stacking reflects a narrow band of wavelengths by interference, so colour comes from structure rather than from a light-absorbing pigment

evidence.citation: Vignolini S, Rudall PJ, Rowland AV, Reed A, Moyroud E, Faden RB, Baumberg JJ, Glover BJ, Steiner U (2012). Pointillist structural color in Pollia fruit. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 109: 15712-15715.

Parker RM, Guidetti G, Williams CA, Zhao T, Narkevicius A, Vignolini S, Frka-Petesic B (2018). The self-assembly of cellulose nanocrystals: hierarchical design of visual appearance. Advanced Materials 30: 1704477.

known_products: Sparxell plant-based structural colour (University of Cambridge spin-out)
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Controlling colour uniformity and scaling up production are still active challenges; colour depends on viewing angle. Commercial products are early-stage.

title: Bird-feather melanin: self-assembled particles for non-fading colour
summary: Many bird feathers get their colours from melanin granules packed in regular arrays, which create colour by interference, while the dark melanin soaks up stray light and makes the colour richer. Synthetic melanin nanoparticles, dried from a suspension, assemble themselves into similar films with colours set by particle size. This points to non-fading, pigment-free colours for coatings, cosmetics and fabrics.
structure: melanin-containing granules (melanosomes) packed in ordered or quasi-ordered layers
mechanism: light reflected from regularly spaced particles interferes to produce colour, and the broadband absorption of melanin removes scattered light that would wash the colour out

evidence.citation: Xiao M, Li Y, Allen MC, Deheyn DD, Yue X, Zhao J, Gianneschi NC, Shawkey MD, Dhinojwala A (2015). Bio-inspired structural colors produced via self-assembly of synthetic melanin nanoparticles. ACS Nano 9: 5454-5460.
Shawkey MD, D'Alba L (2017). Interactions between colour-producing mechanisms and their effects on the integumentary colour palette. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 372: 20160536.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Lab-scale films; durability, skin safety and cost of synthetic melanin for cosmetics are not established. See lib-0037 for iridescent butterfly colour.

title: Saponins: plant soaps that self-assemble into micelles and foams
summary: Saponins are soap-like molecules made by many plants, such as the bark of the Chilean soapbark tree. One end is water-loving sugar chains and the other an oily ring structure, so they gather at oil-water and air-water surfaces, form micelles and stabilise foams and emulsions. Saponin-rich extracts are used as natural emulsifiers in drinks, food and cosmetics in place of synthetic surfactants.

evidence.citation: Bottcher S, Drusch S (2017). Saponins - self-assembly and behavior at aqueous interfaces. Advances in Colloid and Interface Science 243: 105-113.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Extracts vary in composition and some saponins are irritant or toxic at high doses; this record covers their use as an ingredient, not their biosynthesis.

title: Grape pomace: winemaking leftovers as a source of polyphenols, oils and fibre
summary: Pressing grapes for wine leaves skins, seeds and stems, a large seasonal by-product in wine regions such as Spain, France and Italy. Pomace is rich in polyphenols, seed oil and dietary fibre that can be extracted for cosmetics, food and supplements, with the remainder used for compost or energy. Cascading uses turn a disposal cost into several products.

evidence.citation: Beres C, Costa GNS, Cabezudo I, da Silva-James NK, Teles ASC, Cruz APG, Mellinger-Silva C, Tonon RV, Cabral LMC, Freitas SP (2017). Towards integral utilization of grape pomace from winemaking process: a review. Waste Management 68: 581-594.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Pomace is seasonal and spoils quickly, so drying or stabilising it costs energy; extract yields and quality vary with grape variety and process.

title: Olive mill by-products: recovering polyphenols from a polluting waste
summary: Making olive oil leaves large amounts of wet pomace and dark wastewater that harm soils and rivers if dumped, but they are rich in polyphenols such as hydroxytyrosol, valued as antioxidants in cosmetics and food. Gentler extraction methods, such as ultrasound, pulsed electric fields and pressurised liquids, aim to recover these compounds and reduce the pollution load at the same time.

evidence.citation: Rosello-Soto E, Koubaa M, Moubarik A, Lopes RP, Saraiva JA, Boussetta N, Grimi N, Barba FJ (2015). Emerging opportunities for the effective valorization of wastes and by-products generated during olive oil production process: non-conventional methods for the recovery of high-added value compounds. Trends in Food Science & Technology 45: 296-310.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Many of the extraction methods are at lab or pilot scale; the residue after extraction still needs treatment. The Andalusia note is general context, not a finding of the cited review.

source_region.note: Spain is the largest olive oil producer and Andalusia holds most of its olive groves and mills, so these by-products are concentrated there.

title: Gum rockrose: resin and essential oil from Iberian scrubland
summary: The gum rockrose covers large areas of poor, dry soils in the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula. Its sticky leaves give labdanum, a resin long used in perfumery, and an essential oil, and the shrub also offers biomass and other bioactive compounds. Researchers argue it is an under-used local resource that could support rural income in Mediterranean scrubland.

evidence.citation: Raimundo JR, Frazao DF, Domingues JL, Quintela-Sabaris C, Dentinho TP, Anjos O, Alves M, Delgado F (2018). Neglected Mediterranean plant species are valuable resources: the example of Cistus ladanifer. Planta 248: 1351-1364.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Wild harvest must be managed so it does not degrade scrubland habitats; the shrub is highly flammable and its management interacts with wildfire policy. Any traditional harvesting know-how is outside this record.

source_region.note: Gum rockrose scrub (jarales/estevais) is widespread on acid, poor soils of the south-west Iberian Peninsula.

title: Seaweed farming: growing biomass that needs no land, fresh water or fertiliser
summary: Seaweeds are farmed on ropes and nets in coastal waters, growing on sunlight and nutrients already in the sea. The harvest feeds food, cosmetics, alginate and carrageenan production and new packaging materials. Farms take up carbon and nutrients and can dampen waves locally; whether they help the climate depends on what the biomass replaces and where the carbon ends up.

evidence.citation: Duarte CM, Wu J, Xiao X, Bruhn A, Krause-Jensen D (2017). Can seaweed farming play a role in climate change mitigation and adaptation? Frontiers in Marine Science 4: 100.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Carbon taken up is mostly released again when the biomass is eaten or decays, so climate benefit is uncertain. Large farms can shade the seabed, spread disease or alter local ecosystems. See lib-0046 for alginate packaging.

title: Esparto grass fibre: a tough, drought-grown fibre from Iberian steppes
summary: Esparto is a tussock grass of the dry steppes of south-eastern Spain and North Africa. Its long, stiff leaves have been gathered for rope, baskets, matting and shoe soles for centuries, and are still used in Spanish crafts. Tests on the fibres show useful strength and stiffness as a reinforcement for composites, from a plant that needs no irrigation.

common_names: Stipa tenacissima (name used in the cited papers)

evidence.citation: Paiva MC, Ammar I, Campos AR, Cheikh RB, Cunha AM (2007). Alfa fibres: mechanical, morphological and interfacial characterization. Composites Science and Technology 67: 1132-1138.
Fajardo J, Verde A, Rivera D, Obon C, Leopold S (2015). Traditional craft techniques of esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima L.) in Spain. Economic Botany 69: 370-376.
Baz G, Hinojosa M, Quirce S, Cuevas M (1999). Occupational asthma caused by esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) fibers. Allergy 54: 86-87.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The fibre tests used North African (Tunisian) esparto. Craft techniques are cited only to show documented use in Spain; the craft know-how itself is not recorded here and would need the craft communities' consent. Harvesting can damage steppes if overdone; dust from the fibre has caused occupational asthma.

source_region.note: Fajardo et al. (2015) document esparto craft traditions in Spain.

title: Esparto tussocks as nurses for restoring dry, degraded land
summary: In the semi-arid steppes of south-eastern Spain, shrub seedlings planted next to esparto tussocks survived better than those planted in open ground. The tussocks shade the soil, trap runoff water and sediment, and improve soil around them. Using existing grasses as 'nurse plants' is a low-cost way to re-establish shrubs on degraded slopes.

common_names: Stipa tenacissima (name used in the cited papers)

evidence.citation: Maestre FT, Bautista S, Cortina J, Bellot J (2001). Potential for using facilitation by grasses to establish shrubs on a semiarid degraded steppe. Ecological Applications 11: 1641-1655.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The benefit depends on rainfall and species; in very dry years tussocks can also compete for water. Tagged construction-materials for restoring quarries and road embankments in dry areas; this use is our inference, not tested in the source.

source_region.note: Field experiment in semi-arid esparto steppe (Maestre et al. 2001).

title: Traditional solar salt pans: making salt with sun and wind only
summary: In the artisanal salt pans of Aveiro, Portugal, seawater is led through a chain of shallow ponds where sun and wind evaporate it step by step until salt crystallises and is raked by hand. No fuel is burned, and the pans double as wetland habitat for birds and brine shrimp. The process is a working model of low-energy separation and of production that keeps a landscape alive.

evidence.citation: Rodrigues CM, Bio A, Amat F, Vieira N (2011). Artisanal salt production in Aveiro/Portugal - an ecofriendly process. Saline Systems 7: 3.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Output per hectare is low and depends on a dry, sunny season; many traditional salinas have been abandoned. The salt workers' craft knowledge is not recorded here and would need their consent.

source_region.note: Artisanal salinas studied by Rodrigues et al. (2011).

title: Composting: microbes turning manure and food waste into stable soil food
summary: In a well-aerated pile, microbes break down manure, crop residues and food waste, heating it to temperatures that kill most pathogens and weed seeds. As the pile cools and matures, the material stabilises into compost that feeds soil and stores carbon. Maturity can be checked with chemical criteria before use, so immature compost does not harm crops.

evidence.citation: Bernal MP, Alburquerque JA, Moral R (2009). Composting of animal manures and chemical criteria for compost maturity assessment. A review. Bioresource Technology 100: 5444-5453.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Poorly managed piles emit ammonia, methane and nitrous oxide; contaminants in the inputs (metals, plastics) end up in the compost. Tagged packaging because certified compostable packaging relies on industrial composting.

title: Black soldier fly larvae: turning organic waste into protein and fertiliser
summary: Larvae of the black soldier fly eat a wide range of organic waste, such as food scraps, manure and by-products, and grow quickly into protein- and fat-rich insects. The larvae can be processed into animal feed, and their residue (frass) used as fertiliser. Feeding rate and conditions control how much waste is reduced and how much larval mass is produced.

evidence.citation: Diener S, Zurbrugg C, Tockner K (2009). Conversion of organic material by black soldier fly larvae: establishing optimal feeding rates. Waste Management & Research 27: 603-610.
Wang YS, Shelomi M (2017). Review of black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) as animal feed and human food. Foods 6: 91.

known_products: Protix insect protein (black soldier fly larvae)
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Which wastes may be fed to insects reared for feed is restricted by law in the EU; pathogens and contaminants in the substrate need control.

title: Slow sand filters: a living layer that cleans drinking water
summary: Water trickling slowly through a bed of sand forms a thin biological layer on the top, the schmutzdecke, full of bacteria, algae and tiny animals. This layer, with the sand below, removes pathogens and organic matter without added chemicals. Slow sand filtration has supplied towns since the 19th century and is still used where land is available.

evidence.citation: Haig SJ, Collins G, Davies RL, Dorea CC, Quince C (2011). Biological aspects of slow sand filtration: past, present and future. Water Science and Technology: Water Supply 11: 468-472.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Needs much more area than rapid filters and works poorly with very turbid water; the biological layer takes time to mature after cleaning.

title: Tomato peel cutin: a natural waterproof polyester from food waste
summary: Plant skins are sealed by cutin, a polyester made of fatty acids that keeps water in and pathogens out. Tomato processing leaves tonnes of peel rich in cutin, which can be recovered and turned into bio-based, water-repellent films and coatings. It offers a route to packaging barriers from a food-industry waste.

evidence.citation: Heredia-Guerrero JA, Heredia A, Dominguez E, Cingolani R, Bayer IS, Athanassiou A, Benitez JJ (2017). Cutin from agro-waste as a raw material for the production of bioplastics. Journal of Experimental Botany 68: 5401-5410.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Extraction and polymerisation are at research or pilot stage; barrier and mechanical properties are below those of fossil plastics in most tests.

title: Bird nests and loose aggregates: structures that hold without glue and come apart again
summary: A bird nest is a loose pile of twigs and grass held together only by friction and entanglement, yet it is stiff enough to carry eggs and parent. Architects have built walls and domes from loose, specially shaped particles poured into place with no binder, which can be taken apart and reused. Such jammed aggregates are a model for reversible, fastener-free construction.
structure: randomly packed slender filaments or interlocking particles without a binder
mechanism: friction and entanglement at many contact points jam the pile into a solid-like structure, which can be loosened and the parts reused

evidence.citation: Weiner N, Bhosale Y, Gazzola M, King H (2020). Mechanics of randomly packed filaments - the 'bird nest' as meta-material. Journal of Applied Physics 127: 050902.
Dierichs K, Menges A (2016). Towards an aggregate architecture: designed granular systems as programmable matter in architecture. Granular Matter 18: 25.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Aggregate structures are experimental pavilions; they creep under vibration and loads, and are not yet covered by building codes.

title: Polar bear hair: hollow fibres for warm textiles (but not fibre optics)
summary: Polar bear guard hairs have a hollow, porous core that traps air and slows heat loss. A textile made of artificial fibres with a similar aligned porous core kept heat in well in lab tests. A popular story that the hairs work as optical fibres carrying sunlight to the black skin does not hold up.
structure: hairs with a hollow, porous medulla
mechanism: air held in the porous core cuts heat conduction through the fibre

evidence.citation: Cui Y, Gong H, Wang Y, Li D, Bai H (2018). A thermally insulating textile inspired by polar bear hair. Advanced Materials 30: 1706807.
Koon DW (1998). Is polar bear hair fiber optic? Applied Optics 37: 3198.

popular_claim_note: A widespread claim says polar bear hairs act as optical fibres that pipe UV light to the skin. Koon (1998) found that the hair transmits light far too poorly for this, so the claim is not supported.
caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The bio-inspired textile is a lab prototype; real polar bear insulation also relies on underfur, fat and behaviour.

title: Solar parks managed as habitat for pollinators
summary: Solar parks fence off large areas of land for decades, and the ground between and under the panels is usually grass. Managed with native wildflowers, hedgerows and late mowing, it can provide food and nesting sites for bees and other pollinators, and may help nearby crops. Planning this from the start costs little compared with the park itself.

evidence.citation: Blaydes H, Potts SG, Whyatt JD, Armstrong A (2021). Opportunities to enhance pollinator biodiversity in solar parks. Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 145: 111065.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The review identifies opportunities; field evidence on pollinator gains inside solar parks is still limited, and shade and microclimate under panels differ from open fields. See lib-0064 for flower strips.

title: Fish schools as a layout for vertical-axis wind farms
summary: Fish swimming in schools are thought to benefit from the swirling wakes of their neighbours. Inspired by this, researchers arranged vertical-axis wind turbines in tight pairs that spin in opposite directions, so each turbine gains from the flow around the others. Modelling backed by field data suggested such arrays could give far more power per area of land than conventional wind farms with widely spaced turbines.
structure: regular arrangement of swimming fish in a school
mechanism: placing counter-rotating turbines close together lets each one use flow accelerated by its neighbours, increasing power per unit of land area

evidence.citation: Whittlesey RW, Liska S, Dabiri JO (2010). Fish schooling as a basis for vertical axis wind turbine farm design. Bioinspiration & Biomimetics 5: 035005.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. The energy benefit of schooling for real fish is itself debated; the wind farm results come from modelling and small-scale field data. Vertical-axis turbines are less efficient per machine than large horizontal-axis ones.

title: Beaver dams: slowing floods and cleaning farm runoff
summary: Beavers build dams that turn streams into chains of ponds. At a site in south-west England, this stored more water in the landscape, lowered flood peaks downstream and trapped sediment and nutrients washed off intensively farmed grassland. Reintroduced beavers, or dams built to copy theirs, are a nature-based option for flood and water-quality management.

evidence.citation: Puttock A, Graham HA, Cunliffe AM, Elliott M, Brazier RE (2017). Eurasian beaver activity increases water storage, attenuates flow and mitigates diffuse pollution from intensively-managed grasslands. Science of the Total Environment 576: 430-443.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Results come from one enclosed site; beavers also flood farmland, block culverts and fell trees, so reintroduction needs landowner agreement and management.

title: Gas fermentation: microbes that turn steel-mill off-gas into ethanol
summary: Some bacteria live on carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and hydrogen. In gas fermentation they convert waste gases, for example from steel mills, into ethanol and other chemicals, so carbon that would be flared or burned becomes a product. Because it rests on microbial biochemistry, the record waits for legal review before it can be served.

evidence.citation: Liew F, Martin ME, Tappel RC, Heijstra BD, Mihalcea C, Kopke M (2016). Gas fermentation - a flexible platform for commercial scale production of low-carbon-fuels and chemicals from waste and renewable feedstocks. Frontiers in Microbiology 7: 694.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Quarantined: relies on microbial biochemistry, legal review pending. The carbon in the product is released again when fuel ethanol is burned.

title: Snake belly scales: friction that depends on direction
summary: Snakes slide forward easily but grip when pushed backwards or sideways. Their belly scales carry microscopic ridges and fibrils pointing towards the tail, so friction is lower in the forward direction. Such directional textures are studied for sliding machine parts and surfaces that need low friction one way and grip the other.
structure: microscopic ridges and fibril-like ornaments on the belly scales, oriented towards the tail
mechanism: the asymmetric micro-texture catches on surface roughness when moved backwards but slides over it forwards, giving direction-dependent friction

evidence.citation: Baum MJ, Kovalev AE, Michels J, Gorb SN (2014). Anisotropic friction of the ventral scales in the snake Lampropeltis getula californiae. Tribology Letters 54: 139-150.
Abdel-Aal HA (2013). On surface structure and friction regulation in reptilian limbless locomotion. Journal of the Mechanical Behavior of Biomedical Materials 22: 115-135.

caveat: Summarised from the cited literature; not reproduced in a lab; not design advice. Directional friction was measured on skin samples at small scale; transfer to lubricated metal parts such as cylinder liners is still exploratory.
